anchors.fact: Roy Olmstead, a Seattle police lieutenant fired after his 1920 arrest, became the biggest bootlegger on Puget Sound, with a business of bookkeepers, salesmen, drivers and lawyers (HL; LII facts: "not less than 50 persons"). (F2, F5)
anchors.meaning: He knew how things really get done, from the inside.

anchors.fact: He was no saint: as an officer he took bribes and sold probation recommendations, and as a bootlegger he paid off Seattle police and King County sheriffs; the Supreme Court's own facts record his promises of payments to officers (FJC pp. 7, 29; LII). (F3, F4)
anchors.meaning: Must be owned in one plain clause. The reading never implies he was clean; the mirror is the one rule, not the man.

anchors.fact: He did not allow his employees to carry guns, and told his men a lost shipment was better than a lost life (HL, reported speech; HW words it differently). In a trade HL calls "inherently hazardous and violent". (F5, F6)
anchors.meaning: A code stricter than his trade, set for his own people. **Paraphrase only, no quotation marks.** Not "it bound him first" (the rule is recorded for employees) and not "it cost him cargo" (no shipment recorded lost).

anchors.fact: The wiretaps that caught him were a crime under Washington law (1909 statute, a misdemeanor), which the Court's own majority quoted, then admitted the evidence anyway (LII, Taft; Brandeis "wire tapping is a crime"). (F11)
anchors.meaning: The system broke its own rules to catch him.

anchors.fact: The government's own brief, quoted by Brandeis: the Prohibition Unit "disclaims" wiretapping and the Justice Department "has frowned on it" (LII, Brandeis fn). (F12)
anchors.meaning: Even the people with the rulebook disowned the method they used. (Dossier or one clause.)

anchors.fact: Upheld 5–4 on 4 June 1928 (the evidence could stand); Holmes, Brandeis, Butler and Stone dissented (LII). (F14)

Brandeis: officials must be held to the same rules of conduct the law commands of the citizen; when the government breaks the law it breeds contempt for law (LII). Holmes: "dirty business"; better some criminals escape than the government play "an ignoble part". (F15, F16)
anchors.meaning: The person's grievance in the Court's own mouth: the same rule for the people who make it. Paraphrase Brandeis (the "Our government" sentence and our-words rule).

anchors.fact: HL: Seattle would "always" know him as "King of the Puget Sound Bootleggers". (F19)
anchors.meaning: Kills "the code is the part people remember".

anchors.fact: His cargo was Canadian whiskey from British Columbia (HL: "an unlimited source of good liquor in British Columbia"; "nearly 100 cases of Canadian whiskey"). (F2)
anchors.meaning: Base from his trade. HL says nothing about him never cutting his liquor; HW (2023 interview, single) says he didn't cut it "with toxins": legend-grade, signposted at most, never in the bottle as fact.

anchors.fact: Canadian blends came to be called "ryes" during and after Prohibition because so much bootleg came from Canada (*Joy* pdf 423). (E7)

Embury's CANADIAN: Canadian whisky, 2–3 dashes each of curaçao and Angostura, 1 teaspoon of sugar syrup; "Maple syrup is sometimes used in place of the sugar" (Embury, OCR highlight, E2 corrected). Embury held that cocktails should never have more than a hint of sweetness (Oxford pdf 719, E8). Oxford pdf 1226 (Soole): maple "can dominate a drink" (E6).
anchors.meaning: The maple is Embury's own noted variant of this very drink, at his teaspoon. In the reading: "the book notes" (Embury unnamed); the held-back measure rests on balance.py (6.25 ml OUT) and Soole's warning, the sweetness rule stays in the dossier. E4 is a different drink. The stir, coupe, 60 ml and peel are Tomás's.

cocktail.closingLine: Scrape the teaspoon of maple flat. Then show someone close where you draw the line.
method: Put the coupe in the freezer for 10 minutes so it's properly cold.

Measure the maple syrup into a mixing glass or jar: fill the teaspoon, then scrape the top flat with a knife. Add the curaçao and the bitters, pour in the whisky, and stir for a few seconds without ice, until the maple has dissolved. It's thick, and it won't dissolve once the drink is cold.
Fill the mixing glass with ice and stir for 20 to 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass feels very cold.
Peel a strip of orange peel about the length of your thumb, with as little of the white as you can. Hold it skin side down over the drink and squeeze it so its oils fall on the top, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: Where You Stand

recipe.note: any blended Canadian whisky at 40% or a little above; the kind that filled his cases
a flat teaspoon, never heaped: a quarter-teaspoon more tips the drink too sweet. I like a dark one; any pure maple syrup, never pancake syrup
about three dashes, the top of Embury's "2 or 3"

cocktail.tagline: You know how things really get done. You also know what you'll never do.

reading.epigraph: A century ago, Canadian whisky was worth breaking the law for. On both sides of it.
whoYouAre: You know the difference between how things are meant to work and how they actually do: who to ask, what to say, which door opens if you knock the right way. When the official route stops answering, people come to you, and you sort it without a fuss, and without making them feel small for asking.

Behind all that, there's a line. You've got one, and you've never needed to write it down. There are things you won't do, whatever they'd win you, and you keep that to yourself, because out loud it would sound soft. But it's why the people near you feel safe. They may not know exactly where the line is. They know you won't cross it. That matters more than you'd guess: with you, nobody has to wonder where they stand.

What gets to you is the people who write the rules, break them when it suits, and call it procedure. Being pushed around by someone like that, with no say at all, is the nearest you come to being afraid.
yours: Roy Olmstead had been the youngest lieutenant in the Seattle police. In 1920 he was caught bootlegging Canadian whisky and dismissed. He understood the city from the inside: as an officer, he'd taken bribes. Soon, as the biggest bootlegger on Puget Sound, he was the one paying them.

He wasn't a good man by any law's measure. But in a trade that was dangerous and often violent, he had a rule of his own: his men weren't allowed to carry guns. Better to lose the liquor than a life, he told them. Then federal agents tapped his phones, though wiretapping was a crime in Washington State, and in 1928 the Supreme Court ruled, five votes to four, that the evidence could stand.

Justice Brandeis wrote, in dissent, that officials should be held to the same rules the law commands of everyone else, and that a government that breaks the law breeds contempt for it. I like to think you'd have nodded at that. Not because Olmstead was innocent: he'd enforced the rules while letting himself off, and you'd be the first to say so. Because it's what you've always known: whoever writes the rules keeps them too. And even in that trade, his men knew exactly where his line was.

The cocktail I've made for you is the Canadian, from *The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks*, a landmark book first published in 1948. It's straight Canadian whisky, the kind that filled Olmstead's cases, with orange curaçao, Angostura and a teaspoonful of sugar syrup. The book notes that maple sometimes takes the sugar's place. That's the version I've chosen: maple, for the country the whisky came from, one teaspoon exactly, scraped flat. A quarter-teaspoon over, and it tips too sweet. I stir it ice-cold and pour it into a chilled coupe, finished with orange peel. A line, held, in the glass.

You make more of the rules around you than you'd ever admit: who gets helped, and how, and what's never done. So let one person you trust in on where your line is, and let them hold you to it, as you'd hold anyone else. It costs you nothing you'd ever spend. And once someone else can see it, your line isn't a habit any more. It's your word.
